title: Disposition Authority Registry for Chosen Family
one_liner: A verified registry that lets hospitals and funeral homes instantly find out who legally controls a person's body when that person is not the state's default next of kin.
customer: Solo agers, unmarried long-term partners, LGBTQ+ elders, people estranged from family, and blended-family couples pay $59 to register. Estate-planning attorneys, senior and LGBTQ+ service organizations, and hospice or palliative social work teams are the channel and secondary payers.
problem: State statutes rank who controls disposition: spouse, adult children, parents, siblings. An unmarried partner of 30 years can be shut out by a child who hasn't spoken to the deceased in a decade. When it goes wrong, the body sits in refrigeration for days or weeks while lawyers argue, and the funeral home is stuck because releasing to the wrong person means being sued. Many states allow a written designation of an agent, but witness and notary rules differ, and the signed document is in a drawer or a safe deposit box that no one can open at 2 a.m.
solution: Attorney-reviewed, state-specific designation forms completed through a remote-notary and e-sign flow. The signed document goes into a timestamped registry, with a wallet card and a phone lock-screen QR. A 24/7 verification line and API lets hospital social workers, medical examiner offices and funeral homes ask 'is there a designated agent for this person?' The designated agent is auto-notified. The record also stores preferences (cremation or burial, preferred funeral home, link to any pre-need contract).
why_now: The US has a fast-growing population of solo agers and 'elder orphans': never-married, childless, divorced or estranged. The cohort of same-sex couples who married after 2015 is now entering the age of dying. Remote online notarization and electronic signature of estate documents are now widely accepted. Healthcare advance-directive registries exist, but almost none cover disposition.
revenue_model: $59 one-time registration plus $12/year for renewal and verification upkeep. Attorney and organization white-label at $25 per registrant. Hospice, hospital and health-system site licenses at $2,000-$5,000/year for verification access. Verification is free to funeral homes so adoption is frictionless.
non_obvious_insight: The ugliest funeral disputes are almost never about money, they're about who has the pen. Funeral homes carry all the legal risk of releasing to the wrong person, so they will champion and actively check any credible registry. Everyone built registries for the living person's medical wishes, but nobody built one for the body. That is the gap where an insider watches families fight in the arrangement office.
first_30_days: Launch in three states whose statutes expressly recognize a written designation of agent. Partner with a local LGBTQ+ senior center, an elder-orphan or solo-ager meetup, and two estate attorneys who will co-host workshops. Get ten funeral homes to sign a one-page pledge to check the registry on every first call. Sell registrations at senior-center and library workshops and via a 'chosen family' landing page. Target 150-200 registrations and use the first funeral-home lookup as the case study.

title: Dead-Lead Exchange for Solar Installers
one_liner: A reason-coded exchange where solar installers sell their disqualified leads (bad roof, shade, small panel) to roofers, arborists and electricians, with a bounty when the homeowner comes back to buy solar.
customer: Roofers, tree services and panel-upgrade electricians pay per lead. Solar installers receive a revenue share and are the supply side. The end payer is the trade at $60-150 per lead, plus a 5-10% bounty from the installer when a returned lead signs.
problem: Installers pay $100-250 for an exclusive lead and $150-800 for a booked appointment, and CAC is reportedly rising about 40% in 2026. Most of the spend dies at qualification on roof age, shade, roof type or a 100A panel, and the lead is thrown away or resold as an aged inquiry. Meanwhile roofers pay hundreds per closed lead for homeowners who may not need a roof at all.
solution: Installers connect their CRM (HubSpot, Salesforce, JobNimbus, Enerflo) through a webhook. Every lead tagged with a disqualification reason goes to the exchange. A fresh, named-trade consent step, by SMS or a call, offers the homeowner a free quote from a local roofer to make the house solar-ready. The exchange sells the lead to a matched local trade with the diagnosis attached: roof age, photos, shade map, utility bill. When the work completes, the lead returns to the original installer with a 90-day exclusive hold, and the installer pays a bounty if it closes.
why_now: After 25D expired, installers are fighting over unit economics and CAC is climbing, so recouping 30-50% of lead cost matters. Roofers face slower storm work. Homeowners still want solar through TPO, which typically requires 10-15+ years of roof life, so more leads get rejected on roof grounds.
revenue_model: Take 50-60% of the lead price with the rest shared with the installer. Add a 5-10% bounty on returned solar sales. Add a per-seat subscription for roofing and tree companies to get first look in their zip codes. Later, add a financing product that bundles a roof and solar into one loan.
non_obvious_insight: The dead solar lead is one of the best roofing leads in the county. This is a homeowner who was ready to commit five figures to their house, has shown a utility bill, and has just been told by a credible outsider that the roof needs work, so the diagnosis is trusted. VCs treat lead-gen as a commodity, but a closed loop with bounce-back and reason codes is not. The compliance layer (fresh, named-trade consent) is the moat.
first_30_days: Sign 3 installers in one metro who each have 200+ disqualified leads a month. Recruit 3 roofers and 1-2 tree services. Run the whole loop with a spreadsheet, SMS consent scripts and Stripe payouts. Price the first leads at $75-100. Track lead-to-roof-job conversion and how many come back to solar.

title: Hard-Alloy Print Recipes via Sample-Efficient AI Campaigns
one_liner: Sell validated 3D-print parameter recipes and 40-build AI-guided optimization campaigns so ordinary mid-power metal printers can make alloys that normally need rare high-power machines.
customer: Metal additive-manufacturing job shops and small rocket, space and defense suppliers with 400-500 W class printers. University AM labs are a secondary buyer.
problem: GRCop-42, a copper-chromium-niobium rocket-engine alloy, is hard and costly to print. It typically needs high laser power, and about 90% of commercial printers cannot handle it. Every failed build wastes powder and machine time, and shops cannot afford months of trial and error.
solution: A recipe library of machine-specific, validated parameter sets and build reports, sold per alloy and per machine model. It comes with a paid 'campaign' service that uses Bayesian or active-learning search to find working settings in about 40 builds from a few failed starting points. Customer builds feed back into the shared library.
why_now: Washington State University's team used AI to search over 100 million candidate settings, started from 37 failed experiments, and found 6 successful settings in 40 experiments over 3 months, including a first successful print at a record-low 500 W. The work won an Innovative Deployed Application Award, and active-learning frameworks for science are appearing on arXiv (for example arXiv:2609.31197). The method is proven and unlicensed to shops.
revenue_model: Recipe licenses at roughly $5-30k per alloy-machine pair, campaign fees of roughly $20-60k, and an annual recipe-library subscription for shops.
non_obvious_insight: The product is not the alloy but the experiment budget. The WSU study says 90% of commercial printers cannot print GRCop-42 and that success required 'a very challenging case for AI' with rare successes, and the lead author says they are 'essentially democratizing the printing' of the alloy (https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/08/260827010504.htm). Selling failure-avoidance to shops that cannot afford 37 failed builds is a service business, not a materials business.
first_30_days: Contact the WSU authors and WSU's commercialization office about licensing the method. Recruit 2-3 job shops with 400-500 W machines and quote a fixed-price GRCop-42 campaign, with the shop supplying powder and machine time. Pre-sell the first recipe pack to rocket and space startups. Run the first campaign in month 2 and publish a build-report case study.

title: Instant Will-Serve Letters From Hydraulic Models
one_liner: Turn a utility's calibrated hydraulic model into a self-serve 'can you serve this address?' oracle that issues fire-flow and will-serve determinations in 48 hours instead of 4 weeks. It starts with developers and sprinkler designers and grows into a water-readiness index for data center and fab site selectors.
customer: Small and mid-size water utilities and the consulting engineering firms that maintain their models are the sellers. The payers are housing developers and fire sprinkler design firms ($250-2,000 per request), then data center, fab and beverage-plant site selection teams ($20-100k per year for the readiness data).
problem: Every subdivision, sprinkler design and industrial hookup needs a will-serve or fire-flow letter. Utilities own a calibrated hydraulic model (WaterGEMS, InfoWater, EPANET), but one or two engineers, or an outside consultant billing $2-8k per run, can operate it. Requests queue for weeks and stall housing and economic development. Worse, the answer 'we have plenty of water' is meaningless. The binding limits are max-day and peak-hour pressure in one pressure zone, fire reserve storage, tank turnover and water age, and the wastewater plant's discharge limits. Big buyers don't know that, and many utilities can't answer within the time a site-selection process allows.
solution: Ingest the utility's model file (.inp or vendor formats) and pre-compute a grid of scenarios. For each node and pressure zone, calculate available fire flow at a 20 psi residual, the maximum added demand before minimum-pressure or velocity limits break, and the effect on tank cycling and water age. Wrap it in a web form and API: enter address, demand, fire-flow requirement, and get a preliminary letter with the utility's letterhead, assumptions and limits. Exceptions go to the utility's licensed engineer for review and stamp. Utilities set the fee and keep most of it. The large-load layer adds wastewater and pretreatment limits, reclaimed-water availability, drought stage and water-rights status. It is published as a 'water hookup readiness' score by utility, like the power-availability maps that data center developers already buy.
why_now: The data center build-out has made water availability a headline and a local permitting fight, and site selection teams already buy power-availability intelligence but have no water equivalent. Housing permitting reform is speeding the approvals that come before utility review, which makes the utility review the bottleneck. Open-source tooling (EPANET and Sandia's WNTR) plus LLM agents that can read model files and draft letters make productizing this feasible for a small team. Many utilities finished models under recent risk-and-resilience assessments and master plans, so the models exist and are unused.
revenue_model: Utility SaaS of $15-40k per year, or free in exchange for a revenue share on developer fees. Per-request fees of $250-2,000 paid by developers, with the utility keeping 50-70%. Data subscriptions of $20-100k per year to site selectors, land brokers and hyperscaler real-estate teams. A consulting-firm channel where the engineering firm resells to its 10-30 utility clients.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource is not water. It is the one person who is allowed to run the model. The calibrated model is the most valuable unused asset a utility owns, and the answer developers want is hydraulic (peak-day and fire-flow at one node), not a volume in an annual water permit.
first_30_days: Approach one consulting engineering firm that maintains models for 10 or more small utilities and pitch productizing its most repeated task. Build a thin front end on WNTR or EPANET and offer one utility a free pilot: a public fire-flow map plus a letter template. Run the first 20 requests semi-manually, with the engineer generating and signing outputs in the background. Charge local sprinkler design firms $250 per fire-flow letter. Use the results to show turnaround times to two more utilities and to start a data-center-readiness prototype for one region.

title: Operating System For Staff Cooperatives
one_liner: Digitise the exercise-book ledgers of workplace cooperatives, which are the cheapest credit pipe for Nigerian civil servants and teachers, then connect their idle surpluses to each other.
customer: Thrift-and-credit cooperative societies for teachers, nurses, civil servants, police, university staff and market associations. Their executive committees pay for the software. Later, the MFB or bank partner that funds wholesale lending between cooperatives.
problem: Outsiders assume Nigerian salary earners borrow from loan apps or MFBs. In reality a huge share borrow from staff cooperatives at about 10% flat per year, with payroll check-off giving near-zero defaults. But most societies run on Excel, exercise books and a treasurer's WhatsApp. Collapses come from embezzlement, unreconciled employer remittances, and members who cannot see their balances. Some cooperatives sit on idle surplus at 3-8% in a savings account while others in the same city ration loans to a waiting list.
solution: A WhatsApp-first ledger and treasury app: member savings and shares, loan applications with digital guarantors, approval workflows, automated reconciliation of employer check-off remittances against the deduction schedule, monthly member statements, and AGM voting and dividends. AI vision digitises the old exercise books on day one from phone photos. Once ledgers are clean and trusted, add an inter-cooperative wholesale line, routed through a bank or MFB partner, where surplus societies lend to constrained ones at a spread.
why_now: Multimodal AI can now read handwritten ledgers cheaply and reliably, which removes the onboarding barrier that killed earlier software. Tighter FCCPC rules on digital lenders have thinned out predatory apps and pushed members back toward cooperatives. Inflation and salary delays have raised demand for member loans. Open banking and cheaper payout APIs let cooperatives collect and disburse without paper cheques.
revenue_model: SaaS of about N25k-100k per month per cooperative, or N100-200 per member per month. A 0.5-1% spread on inter-cooperative wholesale loans. Fees on embedded products for members (insurance, school-fee financing, phones and gadgets) via the platform.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not capital or customers but trusted records. Once a cooperative's ledger is clean and independent, it becomes a credit-bearing entity and its members can become a distribution channel, which is why the software is a wedge into wholesale lending. The check-off arrangement with the employer is the underwriting moat that no fintech can replicate.
first_30_days: Approach 10 cooperatives through teachers' unions, hospital staff associations and state civil-service networks. Digitise their books free using photo OCR, then start charging from month two. Get an accountant or cooperative-federation officer as a paid advisor for credibility. Track the first reconciliation win, such as finding a missing month of employer remittance, and use it as the case study.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.

title: White-Label Camera Forensics for Cities and Schools
one_liner: Scan municipal and school camera, recorder and IoT fleets to unmask white-labeled hardware with covered Hikvision or Dahua internals and produce grant-ready compliance attestations and phased replacement plans.
customer: City and county IT and police departments, school districts, transit agencies and the MSPs and integrators serving them. They pay $3-15k per fleet audit plus an annual monitoring fee.
problem: Federal grant terms (DOJ, DHS and FEMA, school-safety programs) bar covered surveillance equipment under NDAA Section 889 and 2 CFR 200.216, including where it is a substantial or essential component of a system sold under another brand. Many fleets bought 2015-2020 contain OEM boards nobody can trace, and the integrator who sold them has a conflict in saying so. Sensor stacking (noise detectors on license-plate readers) is spreading while surveillance-vendor scrutiny grows.
solution: An agentless scanner that fingerprints devices by firmware, banners, MAC ranges and cloud endpoints (including peer-to-peer relay services) to reveal OEM lineage across cameras, NVRs, access panels and doorbells. Output is an asset inventory, a grant-attestation letter, and a replacement plan sequenced against grant cycles, with domestic or trade-compliant alternatives. Integrators pay a referral fee for replacement work.
why_now: Compliance is now BOM-level across industries, and grant conditions are being enforced more tightly. Cities face ADA Title II (Apr 2027) and CJIS 6.0 (Oct 2027) deadlines that already force IT audits. Public backlash over camera vendors makes proof of diligence politically valuable.
revenue_model: $3-15k per fleet audit, $1-3 per device per year for monitoring and re-scan, and 3-8% referral fees on replacement projects. Sell through MSPs and state cooperative contracts.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance is defined by the chip in the box, not the label on the box. Origin lineage of white-labeled OEM electronics is an unpriced supply-chain data problem that only shows up at the moment a city touches federal money, and the fingerprint database becomes the moat.
first_30_days: Release a free 'Is my camera a Hikvision?' desktop scanner for IT staff as lead-gen, audit 3 school districts at cost to build the fingerprint set, and then sell $5k audits to the first 5 districts via grant writers and state school-safety offices.

title: The 3 A.M. Pharmacist Desk for Konbini
one_liner: A neutral, multilingual, 24-hour remote pharmacist service that issues the emailed certificate the new law will require before konbini without pharmacists can sell OTC drugs.
customer: Convenience-store owners, first independents and multi-chain franchisees in tourist and nightlife areas of Osaka such as Namba, Dotonbori, Shinsekai and Umeda, then chains. Hotels and hostels are a second channel. Stores pay per certificate, or by sharing the margin on OTC sales.
problem: After 11pm, people keep coming in asking for painkillers, stomach medicine, cold medicine, motion-sickness pills, period-pain relief and allergy tablets. Most Type 2 OTC drugs can only be sold when a registered seller is on the premises, and night staff do not have that license. I turn away a steady stream of tourists and night workers every night. Foreign visitors cannot get counseling in their own language even when a pharmacy is open. That is lost margin and a real public-health gap.
solution: Customers scan a QR code on the shelf, choose products, and join a 60-90 second video or chat consultation in Japanese, English, Chinese, Korean or Vietnamese with a licensed pharmacist. They receive a certificate by email or app, and the clerk verifies it on a phone-based web page before ringing up the sale. The pharmacist network is staffed by night-capable remote pharmacists, such as parents and retirees working from home. The operator holds the pharmacy license and takes on regulatory and liability responsibility. Pre-2027, the same desk runs a limited service on quasi-drugs and pharmacy-hours referral lists so the network and the store workflow are ready when the rule takes effect.
why_now: The amended Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act passed in May 2025. It allows convenience stores without pharmacists or registered sellers to sell OTC drugs after the buyer gets an online pharmacist explanation and an emailed certificate. It takes effect around spring 2027. Lawson has said it plans OTC delivery at stores without pharmacists starting in 2026. Inbound tourism to Osaka remains at record levels. The window for a neutral operator is the next 6-9 months, before chains sign exclusive deals.
revenue_model: ¥300-500 per certificate paid by the store, or 25-30% of the OTC gross margin. Hotels and hostels pay a subscription for guest access. Later revenue comes from manufacturers paying for education and sampling inside consultations, and from chains licensing the network.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for konbini OTC is not shelf space, POS integration or the law. It is a supply of licensed humans awake at 3 a.m., speaking Vietnamese or Chinese, who can explain a drug in 90 seconds. Chains will assume they can build this in-house, but they lack pharmacist labor and multilingual night coverage. A neutral network that any owner can join in an afternoon has the advantage, because independent and multi-chain owners have no other option.
first_30_days: Partner with one licensed Osaka pharmacy, or set up the pharmacy entity, and recruit 10-15 remote pharmacists for night and weekend slots. Build the QR, video, certificate and clerk-verification flow as a web app, tested at my three stores on quasi-drugs and referral flow. Pre-sign letters of intent with 10 owners for spring 2027 pricing. Approach two hotels near Namba for guest access. Meet the health-center pharmacy inspection office to confirm the compliance path before launch.

title: Boundary Truth: Ledger of Special-District Lines
one_liner: Turn recorded annexation, inclusion and exclusion instruments into a single authoritative boundary ledger that catches wrong tax bills, wrong ballots and wrong 911 routing.
customer: County assessors and treasurers, election offices, state 911 boards and NG911 GIS coordinators, plus special-district management firms and metro-district law firms. Paid through the recorder's technology or preservation fund (spendable at the recorder's discretion in many states), election grant money or 911 fee funds.
problem: There are about 39,000 special districts (fire, water, library, mosquito, metro) and their boundary changes are recorded with the county clerk as ministerial filings with no downstream notification. Nobody reliably updates the assessor's tax-area codes, the election office's address-to-district crosswalk or the 911 emergency-service boundary layer. Result: parcels billed by the wrong district or by none (lost revenue, later refunds), voters handed the wrong ballot style, and dispatch mismatches. State attorneys general have issued opinions on tax levies made after officials weren't notified of boundary changes. We discover the errors in the last two weeks before an election or when a taxpayer complains.
solution: An AI pipeline reads the recorded instruments (metes-and-bounds text, plats, ordinances), draws polygons with closure and area sanity checks, and routes low-confidence ones to a human reviewer. It keeps a versioned, effective-dated ledger of each district's legal boundary. It then diffs the ledger against the assessor's tax-area file, the voter address crosswalk and the 911 boundary layer, and returns a plain exception list such as '312 parcels inside Fire District 4 per the 2022 recorded inclusion but billed to no district.' Sell a fixed-price audit first, then an annual subscription.
why_now: Mid-decade redistricting fights and the 2026 midterms have made ballot-style accuracy politically radioactive. NG911 requires clean authoritative boundary GIS data. Property tax scrutiny makes every misbilled dollar a headline. LLMs can now parse legal descriptions well enough to draft polygons that a human reviews rather than draws.
revenue_model: $15k-$40k one-time boundary drift audit per county, then $10k-$30k/year per county for continuous monitoring, sized to fit inside a recorder's technology fund or a 911 board budget. Data-quality add-ons for district management firms and bond counsel.
non_obvious_insight: The legal boundary is the recorded instrument, not the GIS layer; the layer is just someone's drawing of a PDF. Because the clerk often sits at the junction of records, elections and sometimes tax, we see the stale cascade that assessors, election staff and 911 GIS analysts each see only a slice of. Also, the clerk's tech fund often sits outside the commissioners' budget fight, so a $25k audit can be approved in weeks, not the 18 months that scares govtech investors.
first_30_days: Pick one state heavy on special districts (Colorado metro districts, Texas MUDs and ESDs, Illinois, Washington, Florida CDDs). Offer a free boundary drift audit to a single county's assessor and clerk using five years of recorded inclusions and annexations. Turn the mismatch list into a paid pilot funded from the recorder's fund, then take the proof to the state 911 board.

title: Rent Ledger for Adult Kids Living at Home
one_liner: A simple lease, payment and credit-reporting layer that lets parents charge their adult children rent, build the kids' credit history, and quietly bank the money as a down-payment fund.
customer: Parents (Gen X and Boomers) with adult children aged 22-30 living at home, paying $12/month per household. Secondary revenue from mortgage lenders and first-time-buyer programs.
problem: Nearly half (49%) of US adults under 30 lived with parents in 2025, up 12 percentage points from 2019 (Federal Reserve SHED). Only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or a paid-off card, and the Fed reports 16% of adults use buy-now-pay-later, with 11% of users hit by overdraft fees from missed payments. Lender-side data shows BNPL is spreading into groceries (a LendingTree survey reported nearly a quarter of BNPL users financed groceries, up from 14%; 41% reported a late payment). These young adults are paying for hobbies, subscriptions and installment plans while accruing no rent history at all, since informal family housing builds no credit and no savings discipline.
solution: An app that produces a simple parent-child lease, collects a modest monthly 'rent' by ACH, reports on-time payments to the credit bureaus through an established rent-reporting partner (do not become a furnisher), and lets the parent choose to escrow the money in a labeled account toward a future down payment or move-out fund. It gives the kid a monthly statement and a BNPL and subscription view so obligations don't collide with rent day. It includes parent-side documentation of the rent for tax purposes (tax treatment is a gray area, so it needs CPA-reviewed templates).
why_now: The 12-point jump in under-30s living at home is now structural, not a pandemic blip. Rent reporting has been mainstreamed by consumer fintechs and by underwriting systems that count rental payment history, and BNPL late payments are rising, which raises the value of a credibility-building habit. Housing costs make first-time down payments the main goal for these households.
revenue_model: $12/month per household (parent pays), $5/month optional kid add-on for credit-builder features. Referral fees from mortgage lenders and down-payment-assistance programs when the kid buys. Later: employer benefit channel for parents.
non_obvious_insight: Parents are the largest unpriced landlord class in the US, and they already hold the leverage the market lacks: the kid will pay them and will not skip. The product isn't a rent app, it is a behavioral bridge that converts a free-rent arrangement into credit history plus parent-held savings. Evidence: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm (49% of under-30s living with parents, +12 points since 2019; 63% cover $400; 16% BNPL, 11% overdraft fees) and BNPL grocery and late-payment figures via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_now,_pay_later (summarizing LendingTree). Assumptions to validate first: that bureaus and lenders will accept rent reported for a parent-landlord and how underwriting treats it, and that parents want to charge rent and save it. I found no survey on either.
first_30_days: Interview 20 parents in local parenting and finance Facebook groups. Test a landing page and a $12/month waitlist. Run a concierge pilot with 10 families: a lease template, ACH collection, an existing rent-reporting partner and a shared spreadsheet. Confirm with a mortgage broker whether reported parent-landlord rent helps underwriting. Target 15 paying families and one lender-partner conversation.

title: Liquid-Cooling Leak-Test Crews for AI Data Centers
one_liner: A specialty crew of journeyman plumbers that flushes, fills, pressure-tests and photo-documents every quick-disconnect in AI liquid-cooled halls, sold per rack to neoclouds and the contractors building for them.
customer: Neocloud and colocation operators building liquid-cooled GPU halls, and the mechanical and general contractors on those builds who carry the commissioning schedule and the liability.
problem: Liquid cooling for AI racks turns data centers into plumbing systems with hundreds of quick-disconnect pairs per rack and coolant loops feeding hardware worth millions. Leaks at quick disconnects were among the failures during the first field ramps of dense racks. Commissioning delays on a large hall cost on the order of $14M per month, and pipefitters and mechanical trades are named in July 2026 surveys as one of the top three labor gaps. Much of the rack-level wet work is done by data-center technicians and electricians who were never trained in flushing, air removal, test discipline or cleanliness, so tests pass on Friday and a fitting drips on Monday.
solution: A three-person 'wet-work pod' (two journeymen and one apprentice) with a kit: pressure-decay test rig at 1.5x operating pressure, a filtered flush cart with a particle counter, a glycol refractometer, a borescope, UV dye and torque tools. The pod flushes and fills loops, purges air, tests and re-tests, and logs every quick-disconnect with a photo, QR tag and rack serial, generating the traceable leak-test record the lender, the insurer and the operator want. Priced per rack or per pod-day, with a commissioning-window guarantee. Later add a warranty-backed re-inspection after thermal cycling.
why_now: Liquid cooling roughly doubled in 2025 and is forecast to keep compounding, the racks in the field have far higher density and leak sensitivity than air-cooled halls, and the labor gap in pipefitting is the acknowledged constraint. Operators are paying premiums for anyone with liquid-loop experience, and the cost of one leaked rack dwarfs the cost of the crew.
revenue_model: $350-900 per rack for flush, fill, test and documented verification, or $2,400-3,500 per pod-day with a minimum engagement, plus paid re-inspection visits and a documentation package fee. Gross margin of 30-40% after paying journeymen $75-95 per hour, well above residential wages.
non_obvious_insight: Data center people think the hard part is the chip; plumbers know the hard part is water. Air pockets, thermal expansion, dirty new pipe (flux, cutting oil, thread dope), dissimilar metals and untested O-rings are what leak, and a documented test is worth more than a passed one. For a plumbing shop this is also a retention weapon: a road crew at data center rates keeps a 35-year-old journeyman from leaving the trade.
first_30_days: Use permit filings to find three data center builds within driving distance and call the mechanical superintendents. Offer a paid two-day leak-test audit on one row of racks. In parallel finish subcontractor prequalification (OSHA 30, insurance, NDA, background checks) and build the QR-tag and photo log. Put two journeymen from the shop on a rotating schedule so the residential business does not suffer.

title: Booth-Day Cover: Weather-Out Insurance for Vendors
one_liner: A $5-$15 add-on at booth-application checkout that pays vendors their booth fee plus a loss tier when rain, wind, heat or smoky air wrecks an outdoor event day.
customer: Art-fair exhibitors, farmers' market growers, food-truck and craft-fair vendors, sold at checkout through event organizers and vendor-booking platforms.
problem: Vendors prepay $150-$900 in booth fees plus travel and perishable inventory. When an event is rained out, wind-cancelled, or smoke keeps customers home, organizers rarely refund, and event-cancellation insurance protects only the organizer. The vendor is the uninsured party, and smoke-driven closures are increasingly common.
solution: Per-booth-day parametric micro-policies triggered by hourly station and radar data (rain over a threshold during market hours, gusts above a limit, heat index/WBGT, AirNow/PurpleAir AQI at or above 151). Payout tiers of $75-$500 are set by booth fee. Cover is sold via API in the booking checkout. Organizers get a 'weather-safe vendors' badge, a revenue share and a dashboard. Claims are automatic and paid to the vendor's payout account.
why_now: Smoke seasons since 2023 made AQI-linked outdoor closures routine. Hyperlocal sensor networks and 1 km radar rainfall data are cheap. Embedded-insurance APIs make per-transaction cover easy to bolt onto checkouts. A likely very strong El Niño (CPC/IRI, September 2026) points to a wet winter in the southern tier, where winter markets and festival seasons run.
revenue_model: Premium of about $6-$12 per booth-day at a 20-30% loading over expected loss, with 15-20% shared with the organizer or platform. Later, multi-event season passes and organizer-side cancellation cover.
non_obvious_insight: In outdoor events the vendor is the uninsured party, and a booth-day is a near-perfect unit of insurance: known date, place, price and trigger. The checkout is the underwriting file and weather data is the claims adjuster, so there is almost no claims cost.
first_30_days: Pitch two or three regional market associations and one art-fair or festival platform. Underwrite through a parametric MGA. Ship a Stripe checkout link with a simple rain/AQI/wind trigger table. Pilot 100 vendors at about $6 each across fall festival season and publish the first payout story.

title: Transfer-Portal Durability Passport for College Athletes
one_liner: An athlete-owned, verified injury and load history that programs will demand before they commit six figures of revenue share.
customer: College programs (general managers, sports medicine, compliance), collectives and agents pay for verified dossiers; athletes get their file free and own it.
problem: Chain: the House settlement lets schools pay athletes up to about $20.5M in 2025-26, unlimited transfers and the June 2026 shift to a five-year eligibility clock make multi-year, money-bearing roster bets, yet there is no standard electronic medical record across schools. Injury history moves by phone call and rumor: athletes fear disclosure, programs fear buying a torn ACL, and agents cannot prove durability.
solution: A consent-based portal where athletes' athletic trainers upload structured injury and return-to-play summaries, a standardized functional battery (jump/landing, isometric strength, hop tests) run at partner performance gyms, and optional load history exports from Catapult or WHOOP. The athlete chooses who sees what; the receiving program pays for a standardized, verified dossier.
why_now: Revenue-share contracts, unlimited transfers and the 2026 eligibility overhaul raise the financial stakes of injuries; the proposed Protect College Sports Act would add post-eligibility medical coverage duties and privacy protections; state privacy laws and HIPRA push consent-based data handling.
revenue_model: $150-300 per verified passport paid by the receiving program; $10-25k per year per program for scouting and post-signing baselines; $99 per athlete from agents.
non_obvious_insight: The athlete, not the school, must own the file: that is what makes disclosure acceptable and gives buyers something they can trust. It is a Carfax for players, and the customers now have real money at risk.
first_30_days: Recruit 30 mid-major and D2 basketball and volleyball athletes entering the portal through 3-4 friendly agents, build the consent form and one-page dossier, run 10 test sessions at a local performance gym, and pitch three assistant coaches or GMs on paying $200 per dossier.

title: Duty Refund Claims Desk for Small Importers
one_liner: Over $100B in tariff refunds are flowing, but small importers can't afford the paperwork. Run the filing, deadline tracking and refund advance as a service.
customer: Small and mid importers of record ($1M-$50M of annual imports) that paid the struck-down tariffs, plus customs brokers who don't want the grunt work.
problem: Refunds are flowing but small importers face records, liquidation and protest deadlines, multiple brokers and bonds, and filing costs ('not without a cost,' Colorado Sun, 2026-07-02). The government is fighting an order to refund all importers (WaPo, 2026-08-11). Brokers are paid per entry, not per refund, so nobody chases.
solution: Connect customs-entry data from the importer's broker, identify eligible entries and deadlines, file protests and post-summary corrections through a partner licensed customs broker, and track each claim to payment. Offer an advance of about 80% of approved claims at a discount, funded by a small credit facility.
why_now: Refunds have passed $100B (CNBC 2026-08-07, Forbes 2026-09-09) with litigation ongoing. Twenty-five states are challenging the replacement Section 122 tariffs, so a second claim wave may follow.
revenue_model: 10-15% success fee on recovered duties, plus a 2-3% monthly discount on advances once financing is in place.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck isn't law, it's data assembly and deadline hygiene. The refund often lands in a broker's account or gets stuck for lack of a clear owner. Small importers who recover cash are also the source of pass-through claims for the downstream-recovery business.
first_30_days: Sign a licensed customs broker as partner. Recruit 20 importers through marketplace-seller communities and manufacturer associations. Process five entries by hand end to end and collect the first success fees.

title: Forensic Chat-Log Analysis for AI-Harm Lawsuits
one_liner: A court-defensible method and service that turns exported chatbot transcripts into escalation timelines, sycophancy evidence and missed-crisis reports for plaintiffs, defense counsel and regulators.
customer: Plaintiff firms handling AI wrongful-death and psychosis cases, defense counsel at AI companies and app makers, and state attorneys general, paying $10-30k per case plus expert-witness fees.
problem: Trend chain: over a million weekly suicide-related conversations with general chatbots (OpenAI, Oct 2025), then Raine v. OpenAI plus at least nine similar suits, then hundreds of thousands of words of transcript per case with no standard way to measure sycophancy, delusion reinforcement or whether crisis protocols fired. Expert testimony is ad hoc, and the first Daubert-style challenges are coming.
solution: A clinician-designed coding manual plus a software pipeline. It ingests exports from ChatGPT, Character.ai and Replika formats and tags each turn for risk disclosure, model response type (refuse, validate, encourage, refer) and escalation, then produces an evidentiary report with reproducibility statistics and inter-rater reliability from two clinician coders plus model assistance.
why_now: The litigation wave is live, Pennsylvania's Department of State sued in May 2026, the Human Line Project reports members in 22 countries with logs in hand, and no accepted methodology exists yet. Whoever's method survives the first challenge becomes the standard.
revenue_model: Per-case fixed fee of $10-30k, subscriptions for firms with multiple cases, expert-witness and training fees, later insurer and state-AG contracts.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce asset is not AI. It is a validated, adversarially tested coding scheme that survives its first Daubert challenge, like DNA or forensic accounting. Because defense will need the same method, the business is side-agnostic and cannot be undercut by a lab.
first_30_days: Recruit a forensic psychiatrist and a forensic linguist. Code the excerpts quoted in five public complaints to build a v0.1 manual. Offer three plaintiff firms a free two-week pilot analysis on one case each, then convert to fixed fees and publish a methods note.

title: Real-Brine Library and DLE Benchmark Lab
one_liner: A neutral bank of characterised real brines, matrix-matched reference materials and public bake-offs of direct lithium extraction vendors, so nobody has to run a $3M private pilot to compare technologies.
customer: Three payers. First, brine developers (Smackover, Salton Sea geothermal, Argentine and Chilean salars, Utah and Nevada, Canadian oilfield brines) buying screening reports of $15-40k. Second, DLE vendors paying $30-80k per benchmark round for credible independent data. Third, commercial labs paying $2-3k per year for proficiency testing and buying CRMs.
problem: DLE vendors demonstrate on synthetic or 'friendly' brines. Real brines differ in Mg, Ca, Fe, Mn, silica, organics, H2S and temperature. Sorbent life, water balance and reagent cost only show up after hundreds of cycles, so every developer runs its own bespoke pilot ($1-5M, 12-18 months), and claims cannot be compared. On top of that, high-TDS brines (200-400 g/L) are notoriously hard to assay. Different labs disagree by 5-15% because of matrix effects, so 'recovery' computed from assay is shaky. Sealed drums of characterised brine from finished pilots sit unused in every developer's yard.
solution: Collect 12-20 characterised brines, anonymised if the owner wishes, stabilised in sealed drums. Run standardised bench protocols with vendors (50-100 sorption and desorption cycles, membrane or solvent equivalents) and publish scorecards on Li recovery, Mg and Ca rejection, water use, reagent cost per tonne LCE and degradation curve. Sell matrix-matched brine CRMs and inter-laboratory proficiency rounds to labs, and publish a certified-lab list. Developers buy cheap 'technology screening' reports that shortlist vendors before committing to a pilot. Lenders' independent engineers cite the benchmark.
why_now: After the 2023-25 lithium price collapse, investors will only fund bankable, independently verified technology. A wave of DLE technology-selection decisions is happening now in the Smackover, Argentina (RIGI-backed projects), Chile and geothermal brines. The vendor field is crowded and undifferentiated, so vendors will pay for third-party proof.
revenue_model: Vendor benchmark fees ($30-80k per brine set), developer report subscriptions ($15-40k per year), CRM sales, and proficiency-test scheme fees ($2-3k per lab per year), plus certification.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone thinks DLE is a chemistry problem. In practice it is a brine-specific reliability and data-credibility problem, and no one has standard reference brines, so every claim is unfalsifiable. The killers are minor components (silica, organics, Fe and Mn oxidation) that wreck sorbents after 200 cycles, which a fast pilot on an easy brine never shows. The insider knows that the leftover barrel is the asset.
first_30_days: Ask five friendly developers and labs for 20 L of retained brine (leftover after pilots). Characterise each with two labs. Invite three DLE vendors to co-fund a bake-off on one shared brine. Sell an inter-laboratory round to 6 labs at $2k each (about $12k in the first month) and pre-sell a $10k screening report to 3 developers. Publish the interlab bias chart as the marketing piece.

title: Verification Service for Satellite Imagery Authenticity
one_liner: Check whether a satellite image is real, and issue a chain-of-custody certificate for images used as evidence.
customer: Trade-finance banks and collateral managers, property and cargo insurers, sanctions and compliance teams, and newsroom verification desks.
problem: Generative AI can now fake satellite images, and fakes circulated during conflicts in 2025 (prior knowledge). Imagery is increasingly used as evidence for loans against stockpiles, insurance claims, sanctions cases and environmental claims. Fraud incentives rise with that value, and nobody certifies pixels.
solution: A verification API that checks a submitted image against multi-provider archives (free Sentinel and Landsat plus commercial partners) and physical consistency (sun angle, shadows, sensor geometry). Partners can sign images at ingestion with a provenance manifest. Deliver certified 'as-of' extracts for legal use.
why_now: Generative image quality crossed the threshold in 2025-26. Imagery archives are large and multi-source, and providers are looking for premium 'verified' tiers. The briefing notes decision products for regulated buyers remain open.
revenue_model: $20-200 per verification. Enterprise subscriptions of $30-150k per year. Revenue share with imagery providers on verified tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection models age quickly, but archive access does not. The moat is a cross-provider archive and provenance partnerships, not a classifier.
first_30_days: Assemble a test set of real and synthetic images. Build a reverse-lookup against Sentinel-2 and Landsat. Run free verifications for two commodity-finance firms and one newsroom, then convert one to a paid annual license.

title: Ticket Escrow Bot for Fan Communities
one_liner: A payment-escrow bot for the Discord, WhatsApp and Facebook groups where fans already swap tickets, releasing money only when a cryptographically verifiable ticket-transfer email arrives.
customer: Fans aged 18-35 (K-pop, pop tours, esports, festivals, football supporters) trading tickets peer-to-peer, and the community admins and moderators who police scams manually. Fans pay the fee, and admins get a revenue share.
problem: Ticket fraud thrives in fan groups because the only 'proof' is a screenshot, and generative AI now forges tickets, receipts and transfer confirmations trivially. Official resale is distrusted: per the briefing, Oasis tickets went from GBP 135 to 350+ under dynamic pricing, StubHub's World Cup 2026 tickets failed to reach buyers with class actions following, and the UK CMA ordered StubHub to refund 50,000+ customers over drip pricing. Fans therefore keep swapping in groups, where scammers pretend to transfer tickets or sell the same ticket several times.
solution: The buyer pays into escrow. The seller performs the official transfer in the ticketing app (Ticketmaster, AXS, Eventim, Fever and similar). The buyer sends the platform's 'tickets received' email to a unique escrow address, either forwarded as an .eml attachment or through a narrowly scoped read-only mailbox filter for that sender only. The system validates the DKIM/ARC signature, sender domain, event, section and seat lines, and that the recipient is the buyer, then releases funds after a hold for barcode rotation. Extras: automatic enforcement of a group's face-value cap, light seller verification above thresholds, an admin-facing reputation ledger, and cancellation refunds through an insurance partner. Payments run through a licensed platform-payments partner rather than holding funds directly.
why_now: AI-forged screenshots have made image evidence worthless. Per the briefing, Live Nation lost a federal jury verdict on monopolization in April 2026 and resale fees are under fire, the FTC's all-in pricing rule took effect in May 2025, and StubHub's delivery failures have left fans without a trusted route. Ticketing platforms increasingly move tickets by wallet transfer, so signed transfer emails are now standard.
revenue_model: 4-6% fee on escrowed amount, split between buyer and seller, with 0.5-1% shared with community admins. Premium 'insured swap' add-on. B2B API for promoters that want a safe official fan-swap channel.
non_obvious_insight: You do not need to beat Ticketmaster or become a marketplace. Every major ticketing platform already emits a DKIM-signed transfer email that is very hard to fake, a cheap trust anchor no fan-group scammer can produce. The distribution channel is community admins, who already do unpaid trust-and-safety work and will adopt anything that reduces their scam reports.
first_30_days: Pick one fandom with a high-volume swap group (a K-pop tour or a football supporters' group). Run concierge escrow by hand with a payments-platform account and a script that checks .eml DKIM. Handle 100 swaps at 5% and publish 'scams avoided' stats. Onboard 10 admin partners with a revenue share. Check ticketing terms of service per market before scaling.

title: Flash-Heated Graphite Restoration From Anode Scrap
one_liner: Use flash Joule heating to restore spent and scrap anode graphite to usable grade in seconds, giving US anode makers a domestic, non-Chinese feedstock.
customer: US anode makers and cell manufacturers needing non-Chinese graphite (buyers), and cell-plant scrap managers (feedstock sellers).
problem: Graphite is a large share of black-mass weight, and hydromet recyclers typically treat it as waste. China dominates anode graphite, has tightened graphite export licensing, and the US has almost no domestic supply.
solution: A pulsed reactor (flash Joule heating, from academic work at Rice) purifies and re-graphitizes anode scrap at about 3000 K in seconds, using far less energy than conventional graphitization furnaces. The first product is a 100 kg/day pilot line producing qualification samples, with early sales into non-battery markets while battery-grade qualification proceeds.
why_now: Chinese graphite controls, US trade remedies, and rising domestic cell-plant scrap volumes all arrived in the last two years, and flash processing moved from lab papers to pilots.
revenue_model: Tolling or per-kg sale priced against imported anode-grade graphite, plus grants and offtake advance payments.
non_obvious_insight: Graphite is the one battery material that recycling plants throw away while the US has essentially no domestic supply.
first_30_days: License or build a bench flash reactor. Collect 500 kg of anode scrap from a cell-plant scrapper. Produce samples and send to 3 anode makers or national labs for coin-cell testing. File for DOE or DoD SBIR funding.

title: Second Look: Illustrators as Fake-Image Examiners
one_liner: A bench of displaced illustrators and retouchers trained as human image examiners who certify or flag photos in insurance claims, rental deposits, and e-commerce refunds, with written, defensible reasons.
customer: Small and mid P&C insurers, MGAs and third-party administrators, warranty and protection-plan providers, short-term-rental platforms and property managers, and marketplace trust-and-safety teams. $6-30 per reviewed image set or $2-6k/month retainers.
problem: A March 2026 Verisk study found 98% of insurers agree AI editing is fueling digital fraud and 99% have seen manipulated documentation. Only 7% of anti-fraud professionals rated their orgs more than moderately prepared. Detection software returns probabilities, not explanations, and subtle 'vanilla synthetic' edits (a crack added to a countertop) fool adjusters. A claims team can't deny a claim or testify on a '78% AI' score.
solution: A trained reviewer network that triages with detection software, then writes structured, defensible rationales a special investigations unit can use in denials or disputes ('shadow direction contradicts the window; wood grain repeats; crack terminus violates stress geometry'). Reviewers train on a continuously refreshed library of fakes. Reports are usable in SIU files. A 'fake gym' subscription trains in-house adjusters.
why_now: Insurers' alarm about AI-generated claim images is documented in 2026 (Debevoise, SAS, Verisk). Watermarking and labeling rules like the EU AI Act's Article 50 (effective August 2026) bind good-faith providers, while fraudsters use tools that don't mark outputs or strip metadata. Illustrators are among the most displaced creative workers.
revenue_model: Per-image and per-claim fees, monthly retainers, $150-300 expert-report add-ons, training subscriptions, and a white-label human tier for detection vendors.
non_obvious_insight: The best detector of a fake image is a person who could have made it. Fake-spotting is a craft-knowledge problem about why light, material, and structure cannot be that way, and illustrators hold the largest pool of exactly that knowledge. What insurers need is an explanation they can defend, not a probability.
first_30_days: Build a 200-image benchmark of real versus AI-edited damage photos and publish humans-versus-tools accuracy. Recruit 8 illustrators from artist communities. Pitch 3 MGAs or TPAs and one rental-property manager. Offer a paid pilot at about $10 per claim and close the first one within 60 days.

title: Payday-Shaped Pix Automático Cadence for Low-Income Billers
one_liner: A layer on top of Brazilian gateways that designs the recurring-debit cadence (weekly, biweekly, payday-aligned) and consent options at enrollment, so small billers stop losing all-or-nothing monthly debits.
customer: Small Brazilian businesses billing low-income or irregular-income payers on a recurring basis: neighborhood ISPs, small gyms, neighborhood schools, discount-card clinics, motorbike-rental fleets for delivery couriers (to validate first), and insurance or consórcio sellers. They pay 10-15% of incremental collected revenue.
problem: Pix Automático collects the full amount or nothing, with no partial debits. Retries are limited to 3 in 7 days and only if the payer consented. The payer can cancel or edit the mandate up to the eve of the debit, and the mandate cannot change frequency or amount ceiling after authorization. Meanwhile 83.9 million Brazilians were in negative credit standing in August 2026, a record. Monthly lump debits collide with irregular income, and small merchants still chase payers by hand every month.
solution: At enrollment, quote cadence from the payer's income rhythm (weekly for app-paid couriers and informal workers, biweekly for 'vale' and salary splits, monthly for salaried payers) and create the correct mandate with retries-consent and, optionally, credit-line consent. A WhatsApp 'pre-debit rescue' 48-72 hours before each charge lets the payer confirm, move the date to just after payday, pause, or split into a new mandate, instead of silently cancelling in the bank app. Built as an API layer over a gateway that already exposes the retry policy, such as Asaas. Reports per merchant show debit success rate, cancellation reasons and recovered revenue.
why_now: Pix Automático launched in June 2025 and adoption is compounding. Companies had to be able to offer it from 1 Jan 2026, and it is far cheaper than cards and has no chargebacks. About 60% of low-income Brazilians lack credit cards, so account-debit is the only recurring rail for that segment. Most tooling so far is generic dunning, not cadence design.
revenue_model: Performance-based: 10-15% of incremental collected revenue versus the merchant's baseline, or a flat R$149/month for merchants who prefer subscription. Later a per-debit micro-fee and a marketplace of payer-side 'payday buffers'.
non_obvious_insight: The frequency is locked at authorization, so cadence is an irreversible, high-leverage decision at signup, and nobody optimizes it. Because partial collection is not allowed, the only way to fit a low-income payer's cashflow is to change the shape of the debits, not to chase them afterwards. Evidence: PagBrasil reports +182% transactions and +181% new users quarter over quarter from Q4 2025 to Q1 2026, and a coffee subscriber cut churn 25.2% and cost 50% versus cards (https://www.pagbrasil.com/blog/recurring-payments/automatic-pix-2026/). Serasa reported 83.9 million negativados in August 2026 (https://www.shipay.com.br/inadimplencia-no-brasil-como-melhorar-cobrancas/). Rules on no partials, 3 retries in 7 days and cancellation until the day before are at https://celcoin.com.br/articles/vale-a-pena-pix-automatico/ and https://docs.asaas.com/docs/faq-2. The mandate 'cannot change the frequency' and 60% of low-income Brazilians lack cards (https://www.pymnts.com/news/payments-innovation/2025/pix-automatico-debut-opens-brazils-recurring-payments-market-to-millions/). Small billers describe the monthly grind: 'Todo mês alguém precisa lembrar o cliente, mandar mensagem, enviar chave Pix, cobrar boleto atrasado' (https://www.alfadenegocios.com.br/2026/08/pix-automatico-para-pequenos-negocios.html).
first_30_days: Days 1-3: Confirm in the BCB spec which recurrence periodicities are permitted (weekly and biweekly are assumed, not yet verified) and the per-debit fee, since more frequent debits cost more per charge. Fall back to monthly with payday-aligned dates plus split mandates if not. Days 4-15: Build a thin layer over the Asaas API and a WhatsApp pre-debit rescue flow. Recruit 10 merchants from a single vertical, ideally neighborhood ISPs or courier motorbike-rental fleets, through their ERP user groups and Facebook groups. Days 16-30: Run a split test (monthly vs payday-aligned vs weekly) on new enrollments, report debit success and cancellations, and sign the first 3-5 performance-fee contracts.

title: Parametric Outage Cover for Satellite Internet Users
one_liner: A $60 probe network and parametric policy that pays cash when a satellite-dependent operation loses connectivity.
customer: Mines, farms, offshore and maritime fleets, remote clinics and construction firms whose operations run on a single LEO link.
problem: Insiders treat Starlink as a utility. Operator SLAs give small credits, while the customer's loss is stopped production, idle crews or a stalled remote-operations center. Insurers avoid the risk because they have no independent measurement.
solution: Ship a probe that actively tests the customer's link and cross-checks against a global mesh of other probes. That produces tamper-resistant uptime evidence. Sell a parametric policy that pays a fixed amount per hour beyond a threshold, underwritten by an MGA and reinsurers. Add failover advice and an independent uptime scorecard for SLA negotiation.
why_now: Starlink reached 12M subscribers, and enterprise, maritime and rural operations now depend on it. A widely reported global outage in July 2025 (prior knowledge) showed correlated failure is real. Amazon and others are launching alternatives to fail over to.
revenue_model: Probe subscription $30-100 per month per site. Premium about 4-8% of annual connectivity spend once the policy launches. Data licensing to reinsurers.
non_obvious_insight: Correlated single-vendor outages are actually easy to model, and the true blocker was measurement, not appetite. A cheap independent probe network converts an 'uninsurable' risk into a priced one.
first_30_days: Build the probe on a Raspberry Pi and deploy on 50 friendly terminals from RV, farm and maritime communities. Publish an uptime dashboard. Approach two MGAs about a pilot policy and sell probe subscriptions to three fleets.

title: Flat-Fee Estate Close-Out Pods for Middle-Class Heirs
one_liner: A retired probate attorney supervises 2-3 junior associates and an AI workflow to close $200K-$2M estates for a flat fee, filling the gap between a $400/hr attorney and nothing while giving locked-out grads a paid apprenticeship.
customer: Executors and heirs of middle-class estates (a house plus retirement accounts), often a grieving widow or an adult child. Channels: funeral homes, hospice social workers, credit unions and elder-law referral networks. Flat fee of about $3,500-6,500.
problem: Wealth managers chase the top 2% of households who hold $62T of the wealth transfer. Middle-class estates get either a $400/hr lawyer or an overwhelmed amateur executor, and probate takes 9-18 months (unverified practitioner claim). Online will sellers treat probate as an add-on. Meanwhile entry-level paralegal, analyst and ops roles that used to train juniors are vanishing (Stanford: 22-25-year-olds in exposed jobs 19% below trend).
solution: A 'pod' is one supervising attorney (owning the firm, or operating in a jurisdiction that allows non-lawyer ownership such as Arizona ABS or the Utah sandbox), 2-3 estate associates (laid-off analysts, HR, bank-ops people or grads), and AI workflows for asset discovery, creditor notices, date-of-death valuations, account-closure kits and the final accounting. Each pod runs about 25 estates at once. The heir gets one coordinator, a weekly 15-minute call and one checklist. Associates keep a verifiable log of completed estate steps that ladders to paralegal or licensed-paraprofessional status (AZ, UT, WA, OR, MN).
why_now: Deaths are flat (3.07M in 2024) but dollars per estate are rising, and the first wave of transfers is spousal (about $40T heads to widowed women). AI now handles document drudgery well enough to cut hours per estate from a couple hundred to a few dozen, which turns a not-worth-a-lawyer's-time market into a viable flat-fee product. State regulatory sandboxes are more open to new legal service models than ever.
revenue_model: Flat fee, median about $3,900 with tiers by complexity and state. Target 60%+ gross margin at 25 concurrent estates per pod. Channel partners get flat, bar-compliant marketing fees or co-branded membership benefits (not per-referral fees, which most states bar for lawyers).
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck in estates is not legal knowledge. It is 100-200 hours of tedious, deadline-driven admin that nobody will pay $400/hr for and no algorithm can be trusted with alone. AI collapses the hours enough to make flat pricing work, and the supervised junior is the feature, not a cost, because employers now refuse to train them.
first_30_days: Sign one retired probate attorney in one county (probate is local). Hire two laid-off analysts. Get 3 funeral homes and 2 hospice social-work teams to hand out a one-page 'first 30 days after a death' checklist with a booking link. Price at $3,900, run 10 estates in 90 days on a manual playbook, then automate the steps that repeat.

title: Slop-Risk Diligence for Creator-Business Buyers
one_liner: A fixed-price quality-of-earnings report that prices the platform-policy cliff hiding inside a YouTube channel, newsletter or podcast network for sale.
customer: Search funds, micro-PE roll-ups, creator funds and revenue-based lenders acquiring channels, newsletters and podcast networks priced at roughly $200k-10M, and the brokers who sell them.
problem: Buyers price trailing-12-month revenue. But YouTube's Jul 16 clarification demonetizes generic or repetitive content and AI personas on finance, legal and health topics, Snap stopped recommending fully-AI content, and LinkedIn added a slop-report button. A channel can look healthy on the last year's statements and be one policy update from losing its income. Traditional QoE providers and listing brokers do not model this risk.
solution: A five-day diligence package: audit of how content is produced (share of AI scripts, voices and visuals, template repetition measured via embeddings, reused and stock footage), a policy-risk score against current platform rules, revenue concentration, copycat and re-post exposure, strike and claim history, and an 'earnings at risk' range with suggested earn-out triggers. Templated pipeline with analyst review.
why_now: Creator M&A and creator funds are growing (Slow Ventures' $60M creator fund, brokered channel sales), and the July 2026 policy clarifications make the next 12 months structurally different from the last 12.
revenue_model: $2.5-7.5k per report (roughly 1% of deal size), fund subscriptions for 10+ reports a year, and $500/month post-close earn-out monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Diligence prices the past, and the AI-slop rules make the coming year differ from the past one. Policy risk is a new line in an existing budget, so no new budget is needed.
first_30_days: Pull 50 public listings from Flippa, Empire Flippers and Acquire. Publish five free teardowns, then sell $2.5k reports to buyer communities and search-fund Slack groups.

title: Independent Service Roll-Up for Lab Robots
one_liner: Roll up independent service shops for liquid handlers and lab robots, using remote diagnostics and pooled parts to undercut OEM contracts for squeezed academic cores and CROs.
customer: Academic core facilities, small biotechs and CROs running Hamilton, Tecan, Beckman, Agilent and Opentrons fleets; later autonomous-lab operators who need uptime.
problem: NIH turbulence (a grant-cap proposal, stripped grants-staff protections, K99 visa limits) squeezes core budgets. OEM service contracts typically run about 8-12% of list price per year (an estimate) and OEMs prioritize pharma customers. Layoffs at biotechs and tool vendors free skilled field engineers. Downtime costs more as labs become automated.
solution: Flat-fee per-robot subscriptions at 30-40% below OEM, remote log ingestion with AI triage of error codes, a shared refurbished-parts pool sourced from wind-downs, and uptime guarantees. Acquire 2-4 small independent service shops at 3-5x EBITDA to get technicians and customers.
why_now: STAT tracks ongoing NIH instability. Biopharma layoffs (15,000+) and shuttered labs supply both engineers and used parts. More robots are being installed for AI-directed workflows.
revenue_model: $8-30k per robot per year at 55-65% gross margin on contracts, plus parts and time-and-materials, plus multiple arbitrage on acquired shops.
non_obvious_insight: Automation's bottleneck is uptime, not capability. Agent-run labs make downtime costlier, and robot telemetry lets an independent shop beat the OEM on mean time to repair. Wind-down biotechs are a parts supply the OEMs do not control.
first_30_days: Hire 2 ex-OEM field engineers. Sign 5-8 academic cores in one metro at introductory pricing. Buy used spares from wind-downs. Build a log-parsing dashboard for Hamilton and Tecan error logs.
